rationale: The entry's core — that 'shadow of death' names the symbolic way/condition of sin, darkness, and bondage whose end is the grave, standing opposite the shadow of Christ — is carried by the printed texts better than the strongest specific alternative. Psalm 107:10 explicitly welds the phrase to darkness AND bondage ('bound in affliction and iron'), a condition people sit in, not a momentary peril; Isaiah 9:2 and Luke 1:79 present it as a dwelling condition dispelled by Christ's light, and Luke 1:79 supplies the entry's 'Way' language by contrasting it with guidance 'into the way of peace.' Romans 6:23 supports 'wages end at the pit or grave' and the opposing 'gift of eternal life,' and Philippians 2:5-9 supports the 'humbled Way... which leads through death' to exaltation. The 'shaped like His/Death's substance' mechanics are supported as evidence by the chapter's uniform survey of tsel/tselem and by Colossians 2:16-17 and Hebrews 10:1, which literally call the appointed times 'a shadow... but the body is of Christ,' licensing the parallel construction 'shadow of death' as death's cast outline. The strongest counter (deep darkness/mortal peril) either agrees with the entry's referent in its NT-strand form (spiritual darkness, sin, bondage apart from God — a reading the common interpretation itself lists as prominent) or, in its narrow peril form, fails to explain the 'sitting/dwelling/bound' texts as well as the entry does. No supplied text is explained by the counter that the entry's core cannot explain.
book_core_identification: 'Shadow of death' is not merely gloom or momentary mortal peril but the symbolic way and lived condition of the world apart from God — sin, darkness, and bondage — patterned after death and ending at the grave, the structural opposite of the shadow of Christ.
book_secondary_elaborations: The 'wages' of this way end at the pit or grave (Rom 6:23).
Its opposite, the shadow of Christ, consists of the appointed times, assemblies, and the humbled Way shaped like His substance (Col 2:16-17 via chapter; Phil 2:5-9).
The shadow of Christ leads through death to the gift of eternal life (Phil 2:8-9; Rom 6:23).
Each shadow is shaped like its casting 'substance' (shadow-mechanics: tsel/tselem; Col 2:17's shadow/body pairing).
chapter_only_objections: The chapter's argument that Colossians 2:16-17 protects feast-keepers rather than discharging the feasts (an anti-supersessionist application) is a chapter-level claim, not printed in the entry.

The chapter's broader thesis that 'shadow' in Scripture uniformly means shelter/defence (tsel as 'defence' in Numbers 14:9; Ecclesiastes 7:12) is an argument for the mechanics, not an entry assertion.
Chapter 16's annihilationism, soul-mortality, and 'second death' arguments (Heaven and Hell) are cross-referenced evidence, not assertions of this entry.
The tselem/tsel etymological link ('image' built on 'shade') is a philologically contestable chapter argument.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The lexical-traditional composite: tsalmaveth means 'deep darkness' (or, traditionally, the looming shadow/threat of death), so the phrase symbolizes extreme darkness and mortal peril — the near presence of death through which the believer passes safely under God's protection — with the prophetic/NT strand extending it to spiritual darkness apart from God dispelled by Christ. On this reading 'shadow' is simple gloom, not an outline cast by a personified Death-substance, and there is no structured opposition to a 'shadow of Christ.'
counter_core_identification: 'Shadow of death' = deep darkness/mortal peril, the death-threatening extremity of experience (and, in the NT strand, the spiritual darkness of humanity apart from God), with no substance-casting mechanics or systematic antithesis to the shadow of Christ.
material_core_denial: To become a true rival, the counter must deny that the phrase names a lived way/condition of sin and bondage ending in death, insisting instead that it is only situational gloom or the immediate threat of dying — but Psalm 107:10 ('sit... bound in affliction and iron'), Isaiah 9:2 ('dwell in the land of'), and Luke 1:79 ('sit in... shadow of death,' opposed to 'the way of peace') present a dwelt-in condition of darkness and bondage relieved by Christ's light, which is the entry's referent; the counter's own prominent NT strand concedes that referent.
counter_case: Modern lexicography (BDB/HALOT) revocalizes tsalmaveth as tsalmut, 'deep darkness,' with no etymological link to death, undercutting a 'Death's substance' construction.
Psalm 23:4's pastoral use overwhelmingly reads the valley as mortal danger or the experience of dying, not a worldly 'way' of sin.
No verse states that Death is a body casting a patterned shadow; the substance/shadow mechanics come from Colossians 2:17, which concerns the feasts, not death.
Jeremiah 2:6 and Job's usages describe literal wilderness gloom and the grave's darkness, fitting simple 'deep darkness' without symbolic system-building.
book_explanatory_advantages: Explains why the phrase is something people 'sit in,' 'dwell in,' and are 'bound' within (Ps 107:10; Isa 9:2; Luke 1:79) — a condition/way, not a passing peril.
Explains Ps 107:10's explicit triad of darkness, bondage, and (in context) rebellion matching the entry's 'sin, darkness, and bondage.'
Explains Luke 1:79's antithesis: those in the shadow of death are guided 'into the way of peace' — two opposed Ways, exactly the entry's structure.

Explains why deliverance is always by light shining (Isa 9:2; Luke 1:78-79; Amos 5:8 in chapter): a shadow implies a light behind a body, so the shadow of death itself testifies to the morning — a mechanic the mere-gloom reading leaves as loose metaphor.

The paired construction is textually grounded: Scripture itself calls the appointed times 'a shadow... but the body is of Christ' (Col 2:16-17; Heb 10:1), so 'shadow of X shaped like X's substance' is Scripture's own grammar, applied symmetrically to tsalmaveth.
Rom 6:23 and Phil 2:5-9, printed with the entry, cleanly supply the two ends: wages of the death-way vs the humbled way through death to eternal life.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Philologically safer: 'deep darkness' requires no personification of Death as a substance.
Matches the dominant devotional use of Psalm 23:4 (funerals, dying, mortal peril).
Requires no cross-corpus symbol system; each occurrence can be read locally as gloom or danger.
decisive_sources: Psalm 107:10, 14 — shadow of death paired with darkness and iron bondage, and deliverance as bands broken
Luke 1:78-79 — sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, opposed to being guided into 'the way of peace'
Isaiah 9:2 — dwelling in the land of the shadow of death, relieved by light
Romans 6:23 — wages of sin is death; the gift is eternal life
Philippians 2:5-9 — the humbled way through death to exaltation

Chapter 17 survey: tsel rendered 'defence' (Num 14:9; Eccl 7:12), shadow as covering attached to a body, and Colossians 2:16-17 / Hebrews 10:1 shadow/body-of-Christ pairing supplying the substance-shadow mechanics
unresolved_objections: 'Death's substance' as the casting body is an inference from the shadow/body grammar of Colossians 2:17 and from tselem/tsel, not a claim any single verse states of death.
The lexical revocalization tsalmut ('deep darkness') remains a live philological alternative, though it does not defeat the condition-of-sin-and-bondage referent carried by Ps 107 and Luke 1.
The identification of 'assemblies' within the shadow of Christ leans on the chapter's Colossians 2 reading, whose fuller defense belongs to a chapter-level review.
